edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   [page number alone at right margin]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' (e.g. K1-1) on all six pages instead of a bare page number at the right margin.

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a shape of its own. [3 small hexagons for its 2 coverings, 4 long hexagons for its 3 coverings]
edits.fix: A K-1 child will fill the spare outline with a rotated duplicate and assume that finishes the task. Keep the spares but tell the adult (off the page) that the answers are 2 and 3 ways, so the adult can ask whether the last outline really shows a new way.

edits.quote: Draw each way on a small shape. [8 recording hexagons at half size, about 0.5-inch triangles]
edits.fix: Kindergartners cannot reliably draw rhombus outlines on half-inch triangles. Print 6 or 7 recording outlines at 3/4 or full size, using a second page if needed, or have children color each rhombus. Keep one spare, not two.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 set. All six problems use actual-size boards, and every answer checks: Problem 1 has three coverable and three impossible shapes, including an 8-triangle trapezoid that fails on the up/down count; Problem 2 needs 2/3/4 greens; Problem 3 has 2 and 3 coverings; Problem 4 needs at least 3/3/4 blocks; Problem 5's winning seats are first/second/first/first/second; Problem 6 has 6 coverings. There is enough for well over forty minutes. The fixes are small: the footer, a note about the spare outlines in Problem 3, and recording boards in Problem 6 large enough for five-year-olds to draw on.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   [page number alone at right margin]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all seven pages.

edits.quote: Then explain why nobody can cover the biggest triangle with fewer green triangles than you used. [page 3 shows triangles of side 2, 3, 4; the side-5 triangle and the answer lines are on page 4, which has no problem label]
edits.fix: On page 3 the largest triangle a child can see has side 4, so they may explain the wrong one. Put the side-5 triangle and the 'explain why' sentence together on page 4, starting it with 'Problem 3 (continued):', or say 'the side-5 triangle on the next page'.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side. If you cover it with blue rhombuses and green triangles, what is the fewest number of green triangles you need? What if the board has 100 small triangles along each side?
edits.fix: After Problem 3's 2, 3, 4, 5 pattern, children can answer this in half a minute just by extending the pattern. Fold it into Problem 3, or ask the substantial question: how do you know 10 green triangles are enough, not only that fewer cannot work?

edits.quote: Find a rule that tells which places for the two green triangles work, and explain why your rule is right.
edits.fix: The rule is one up-triangle and one down-triangle. I checked all 144 such placements and every one can be covered, but proving that half is beyond grades 2-3. Ask children to explain why placements that break the rule can never work, and leave the 'always works' half to the adult notes.

grades-2-3.summary: An excellent development of kernel 1. It moves through odd area, unequal up/down counts, a split board (F), holes (E impossible, G possible), the fewest greens for triangles of side 2-5, the chevron comparison (4, 5, 4, 5 greens, never fewer than with blues), a design-a-board challenge (solvable), and a rule for two green triangles. Every board is drawn correctly at actual size, and there is ample work. The remaining edits are the Problem 3 page break, the thin Problem 4, and asking for a proof that is right for this age in Problem 7.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   [page number alone at right margin]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all seven pages.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again.
edits.fix: Copying the six coverings again is busywork. Have children number their Problem 1 drawings and draw the flip connections as a diagram of numbered dots, which also shows the diamond shape. Drop or shrink the eight copy boards.

edits.quote: Find a way to do this with 4 flips that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row. Can you do it with 5 flips? With 7 flips? [two answer lines only]
edits.fix: Children have no way to record which hexagons they flipped. Add a small drawing of covering A where they can number the hexagons they flip, or four small hexagon outlines for the loop. (A 4-flip loop exists; 5 and 7 are impossible.)

edits.quote: Write the ribbon of each covering of the board from Problem 1. On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges. Find exactly what one flip does to the ribbons.
edits.fix: Name the hexagon coverings to study (A-F from Problem 3) and say where to write the ribbons, for example under each drawing in Problems 1 and 3. Four ruled lines cannot hold six ribbons plus the hexagon pairs and the rule.

edits.quote: Then find the fewest flips that change covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: Problem 3 already asks for the E-to-F count (it is 8). Rewrite as: 'Then explain why nobody can change E into F with fewer flips than you found in Problem 3.'

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below [25 outlines with roughly 0.3-inch triangles]
edits.fix: Drawing all 20 coverings (240 rhombi) on 0.3-inch triangles is mostly copying. Let children record each covering by its pair of ribbons, and keep fewer, larger outlines for checking a few.

edits.quote: How many different ways can blue rhombuses cover this board? Explain how you know. [hexagon with sides 1, 3, 3: one ribbon, C(6,3) = 20 coverings]
edits.fix: This one-ribbon count follows directly from Problems 1 and 5 and is easier than Problem 7, where two ribbons must not cross. Swap Problems 7 and 8 so that the one-ribbon count comes first.

grades-4-5.summary: A rich and correct development of kernel 2. Problem 1 has 6 coverings and the farthest pair is 4 flips apart. All six reference coverings in Problem 3 are valid, with fewest flips of 3, 4 and 8. Covering A has a 4-flip loop, and odd loops are impossible. The ribbon example LRRLR is drawn correctly, and the two counts are 20 (hexagon) and 20 (sides 1-3-3 board). The text is clean. The edits are about recording: recopied coverings, no space to record the Problem 4 loop or the Problem 5 ribbons, 20 coverings on tiny outlines, and Problem 8 placed after the harder Problem 7.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 band takes the coloring argument through a well-chosen run of contrasting boards (odd area, unequal counts, a split board, holes, fewest greens, chevrons, designing a board, and the two-green rule), and every board and answer checks out.
overall.weakest: Recording logistics: grades 4-5 recopy coverings, lack space to record the Problem 4 loop and the Problem 5 ribbons, and must draw 20 coverings on 0.3-inch outlines, while K-1 Problem 6 asks kindergartners to draw on half-size boards.
